 Millions of Americans send in a car payment, a student loan payment, or a personal loan installment every month. That money goes to lenders, and some of those lenders hand a large share of their profits back to shareholders as dividends. For income investors, the question is simple: what does it pay to own the companies on the other side of the loan? 
 welcomia / iStock via Getty Images Splitting $90,000 equally across three consumer lenders (one focused on auto loans, one on personal loans and one on student loans) generates $6,464 of passive income a year. That figure uses each company's latest regular quarterly dividend, annualized, at Monday morning's delayed prices. Below is the income a $30,000 position in each of these three high-yield names would produce, ranked from lowest yield to highest. 
 Ally Financial: Auto Loans, an Online Bank and a Fresh Dividend Raise 
 Stock #3: Ally Financial ( NYSE:ALLY ) 
 Yield: 3.65% 
 Shares for $30,000: 783.1 
 Annual Passive Income: ~$1,096 
 Ally is one of the country's biggest auto lenders, working with about 21,600 active dealers. It also runs the largest all-digital bank in the U.S., whose $144 billion in retail deposits make up 87% of its funding. Ally is a regular operating company, so no rule forces it to pay out its income. Its yield is mostly a function of the share price, which is down 12.84% year to date at $38.31.

 The latest quarterly dividend rose to $0.35 from $0.30, a payout that had stayed flat since early 2022. Earnings easily cover it: second-quarter adjusted EPS came in at $1.21, and Ally also bought back $295 million of stock through the first half. The main risk management has identified is tariffs, which could affect vehicle values and demand. 
 Story Continues OneMain Holdings: Personal Loans to Borrowers With Imperfect Credit 
 Stock #2: OneMain Holdings ( NYSE:OMF ) 
 Yield: 7.59% 
 Shares for $30,000: 542.0 
 Annual Passive Income: ~$2,276 
 OneMain makes installment loans to nonprime borrowers (people whose credit scores sit below the best levels) through more than 1,300 branches and a digital platform. It has also been growing its auto finance and credit card businesses. The ultra-high yield shows how investors price lending to riskier borrowers, and the shares at $55.35 are down 11.84% year to date. 
 The $1.05 quarterly dividend sits below third-quarter adjusted EPS of $1.51, and the company generated $284 million of capital in the quarter. Losses are the main risk here. The net charge-off ratio was 6.89%, an improvement from 7.77% in the second quarter, yet provisions for future losses rose to $615 million. 
 Navient: Student Loans and the Highest Yield of the Group 
 Stock #1: Navient ( NASDAQ:NAVI ) 
 Yield: 10.31% 
 Shares for $30,000: 4,830.9 
 Annual Passive Income: ~$3,092 
 Navient manages a shrinking portfolio of older student loans, including about $25.9 billion of federally guaranteed FFELP loans, and makes new refinance, in-school, and personal loans through its Earnest brand. Earnest originations rose 77% year over year to $1.4 billion. 
 A very high yield often signals a low share price and worried investors, and that fits Navient. The stock trades at $6.21 and is down 47.13% year to date. The $0.16 quarterly dividend has held steady since 2015, but coverage is thin. Third-quarter GAAP EPS was $0.16, and Core EPS was $0.03. Navient also has $0.7 billion of senior unsecured notes coming due within 12 months, and S&P has moved its outlook to negative. Thin coverage and a double-digit yield are two of the classic warning signs we cataloged in a free report on dividend traps. 
 One Risk Ties All Three Together 
 All three face borrower credit risk, but Navient's federally guaranteed FFELP loans have government protection that ordinary auto and personal loans do not. A weaker job market or rising delinquencies would hit auto loans, personal loans, and student loans together. The trends look stable for now. Ally's retail auto charge-off rate improved to 1.57%, OneMain's 30+ day delinquency fell to 5.34%, and Navient's 90+ day delinquencies dropped to $274 million.

 Together, these three positions generate $6,464 in annual passive income on a $90,000 investment, a combined yield of 7.18%. Navient contributes $3,092, OneMain adds $2,276, and Ally rounds out the group with $1,096. 
 Lenders can pay shareholders well, since collecting interest on consumer debt makes steady cash. Still, all three of these stocks depend on the same group of borrowers. A portfolio built only from lenders carries one concentrated credit risk, and income investors usually pair names like these with dividend payers from unrelated industries.
